question: Cancer cases have been increasing steadily for decades as a result of environmental factors and people’s lifestyles. That increase has accelerated dramatically since 2021, however, particularly among young people. Between 1980 and 2013, the number of people aged 15-49 dying from cancer slowly decreased, and between 2014 and 2020 it remained roughly constant at a low level.

But between 2021 and 2023 an alarming trend emerged: for the first time in over 40 years, cancer deaths in that age group worldwide shot up: there was an increase of 8.3 % in the space of just three years. A comprehensive review of scientific literature – covering 69 studies from 27 countries – showed a close temporal relationship between cancer cases and COVID-19 vaccinations.

What is more, the US Centers for Disease Control’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices has officially identified four main mechanisms of the mRNA COVID-19 vaccination that can cause cancer. 1.
In the Commission’s view, what has caused the explosion in cancer rates among young people since 2021?
What view does the Commission take of the suspicion that the rise in cancer rates among young people was caused by COVID-19 vaccinations?
What does the Commission intend to do to analyse and stop the increase in cancer cases among young people?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) The Honourable Member refers to a scientific article describing rare, retrospective, temporally associated patterns rather than rigorous, prospective, multidisciplinary research to determine causality1.

In the Commission’s replies to Parliamentary Questions E-002078/20252 and E000093/20263, it detailed that there is no scientific evidence of any increase of cancer occurrence following COVID-19 vaccination. Based on the official data from the European Cancer Information System (ECIS), there is no evidence either of an ‘explosion’ or sudden spike in cancer rates among young people since 2021.

As indicated in the Commission’s reply to PQ E-000972/20264, data enabling robust analysis and conclusions from 2021 will only become available in ECIS in the second half of 2026, following the 2026 update with incidence data up to 2024.

Broader evidence shows so far a gradual long-term increase in some types of early-onset cancers (typically defined as cancers under age 50), with important differences by cancer type, sex, and country/registry5. There is no evidence of sharp discontinuity around 2021 visible in the published ECIS indicators or the broader epidemiology literature.

Instead, studies show a slow upward trend over many years, often beginning well before 2020. The Horizon Europe Cancer Mission6, working in synergy with Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan7, translates evidence generated through research and innovation (R&I) into concrete solutions for people at risk of or living with and beyond cancer and supports Member States in delivering efficient cancer control strategies.
This includes supporting R&I to identify environmental and lifestyle risk factors8 that contribute to the development of cancer in younger age groups.

8 HORIZON-MISS-2027-06-SOIL-CANCER - Living labs to monitor and mitigate carcinogenic substances in and originating from soils: Evaluating their effects on human cancer risks; HORIZON-MISS-2026-02 CANCER-01 - Virtual Human Twin (VHT) Models for Cancer Research; HORIZON-MISS-2025-02-CANCER02 - Understanding the effects of environmental exposure on the risk of paediatric, adolescent and young adult cancers; HORIZON-MISS-2021-CANCER-02-03 - Better understanding of the impact of risk factors and health determinants on the development and progression of cancer.
